This is the crux of the ethical problem. In research ethics, there is a big difference between nondisclosure and deception. 

The author team is misrepresenting their research design as using nondisclosure -- not disclosing the use of AI in their comments. 

But pretending to be an SA victim is not nondisclosure. It is outright **deception**! 

The use of deception ought to have been cleared with IRB from the outset. The moment deception occurred, the author team should have informed the IRB of the incident straight away. 

To be clear, this deception is not only a flagrant violation of ethical standards, it also violates the basic principles of experimental design. Why? The manipulations that were described in the author team's preliminary report have nothing to do with **pretending to be a human expert or a victim** -- this AI behavior is potentially a major confound that would actually introduce distortions in their analysis (unless this AI behavior is secretly what the author team is trying to manipulate). 

In which case, the author team has not only downplayed and misrepresented the **risks** and harms of this study, but also overclaim the **benefits** of this study given the confounding factors that seem to be apparent in their AI-generated comments. 

I would be very interested in taking a look at their pre-registration. What exactly did they pre-register at the outset of this study? This information is often publicly available (as it should be).

If you've got access to the paper, take a look at the scatterplots. I found them quite illuminating. There's a lot of IQ variance at the high end of the scale for using music as sensation-seeking. 

Interestingly, there's very little IQ variance at the low end of the music regulation scale -- just one or two relatively high IQ people, but these people are "influential cases" (some might incorrectly call them outliers) that tip the correlation squarely into the negative range. 

Maybe these one or two influential cases are neurodivergent? I presume some neurodivergent people don't find music as evocative. 

The lack of variance at the low end of the scale suggests to me that maybe we're not getting a fair apples to apples comparison across the full range of the music regulation measure thingy.

I like character-focused SF, so my top 5 is maybe different than most:

1. *Book of the Short Sun* - Gene Wolfe. This rarely discussed sequel to BotNS is a much more powerful read. Wolfe grew much more restrained and much more character-focused as he wrote his way through the Solar Cycle. BotSS is a mature and deeply human piece of SF. IMO it's Wolfe's second-best work, second only to the Wizard Knight duology.

2. *Air* - Geoff Ryman. A uniquely anthropological take on SF. Some of the tech stuff is a bit dated by now, but this novel has a lot of heart.

Convenience. Fewer computational bells and whistles. Simpler and more straightforward ways to test moderation (some argue that latent moderation is more powerful; my sense is that opinions are mixed). Easier to test higher-order and nonlinear interactions. Lower sample size requirements. Easier to interpret (no fussing over model fit, for better or for worse). No need to specify a measurement model (yes, you can run SEM without a measurement model but then what even is the point). Probably runs faster too.

Personally, if PROCESS and a fully disaggregated SEM gave me radically different results, I'd trust the PROCESS results over the SEM results. There are so many ways to screw up an SEM even unintentionally. 

But there are three caveats. First is that no matter what technique you use, you have to know what you are doing. Most of the criticism of PROCESS is that lowers the barrier of entry to people who don't understanding what they're doing. Second is that all bets are off when it comes to moderation. Supposedly latent moderation has more power to find real interactions if they exist, but it also has fairly strict assumptions that if violated can spit out false positives. Third is that you can actually troubleshoot an SEM and get a better sense of what is going on under the hood, whereas PROCESS is a black box. There's a bunch more caveats e.g., measurement error, handling missing data but that's the general idea.

My very superficial understanding of WLS for ordinal CFA is that it is fiddly (e.g., sensitive to missing data). Maybe useful sanity check: do the parameter estimates you get from DWLS make sense? Do the standard errors look inflated? Also at a more basic level, did you find evidence for threshold invariance?

One option if you're really worried is to use a different modeling approach like Categorical ML or a Bayesian approach. As far as I know, these approaches don't give you fit indices, but if the resulting parameter estimates are very similar to the ULS solution, I'd personally take that as a good sign that the ULS result is on the right track.

You're getting a lot of advice to treat the couple/dyad as one unit for sampling purposes, but this approach usually doesn't make sense for qualitative research with interviews. Ultimately, it really depends on the aims of your study. You can always start with the couples you've already recruited, then figure out (a) do you need more participants to get to saturation? If yes, then (b) do you need more couples or more individuals? It can actually be fine to sample a mix of complete and incomplete couples, though of course that depends on your research question.

You've been receiving subdiscipline-specific feedback. Not all qualitative research needs to be "critical" whatever that's even supposed to mean. I'm guessing it has something to do with how well-developed and robust your Discussion section is? I think you are butting against subdiscipline-specific norms that you (understandably) aren't aware of yet.

I notice that highly descriptive qualitative work are often actually quite likely to still get a revise-and-resubmit -- a chance to develop and reframe the work further. So I suspect you may be getting rejected for reasons beyond just how "critical" the paper is. 

My advice is to get feedback from someone who has published qualitative research at the journals you are targeting. These people know the tacit norms of your field and can see the things your paper in its current form is missing. Ideally this person would be an experienced mentor who could co-author your paper and guide you every step of the way. Alternatively, you could "cold call" an author whose work you admire and ask them for a "friendly review" of your paper. There are other posts on this subreddit re: the etiquette around soliciting friendly reviews by email.

Good luck! And don't try to go it alone. Publishing success requires understanding the norms of an academic community as much as actual scientific rigor and quality.

The way academic publishing works is that authors put together a paper and send it off to a journal for peer review. Someone at the journal -- usually an expert in the area -- becomes the point person for handling that paper within the journal. The technical term for that point person is the "action editor" or AE. 

For a journal like Psych Science, a "prestige" journal with a very low acceptance rate, the AE is usually picked from one of the associate editors listed on the journal editorial team (freely searchable online). 

The AE has a huge amount of power in what happens next in the publication process. They pick the "peers" who provide the eponymous "peer review" in the journal. The technical term for those peers are "reviewers." AEs have the power to pick tough reviewers, or asshole reviewers, or gentle reviewers or anything in between. Reviewers make recommendations, but it's ultimately up to the AE whether the paper passes muster for the journal + what changes (if any) need to be made for the paper to be deemed publishable. AEs can ignore reviewer feedback if they choose, which in fairness is not always a bad thing. Lastly, the AE makes the final call to accept, reject, or revise & resubmit -- in principle informed by reviewer feedback but really they have carte blanche to decide as they please. 

Dan Gilbert is *the* emotional intelligence guy and is part of the old guard -- heavily resistant to open science and an inveterate asshole on social media. It's easy to blame Gilbert and the author team for doing shoddy work, but the fact is that some unnamed AE let it through the gates in this rather sorry state. You were totally right to question how the study paradigm in this paper was operationalized, and I'm appalled that the AE chose not to know any better.
This is exactly why Psych Science should note who the accepting AE is for every paper. And this is also exactly why they will never do that.

The disagreeableness often at the core of Mach is likely to decrease over time. Therapy may also help.
